decisions.reason: Toomer (2019; shipped row 2422 year_r=2021; duplicate row 2456 removed) Experiment 2 (Ch. 4) conceptually re-tests Gitsaki’s (1999) specific empirical finding that previously encountered V+N collocations yield lower gap-fill scores than prep+N collocations. Section 2.1.1 (p. 9) attributes to Gitsaki (1999) an empirical study of 275 Greek junior high school learners tested on textbook collocations where gap-fill production was less accurate for V+N than prep+N. Experiment 2 tests 78 Chinese learners on 43 analysed (21 V+N, 22 prep+N) collocations repeated six times under bolded vs. unbolded reading; gap-fill accuracy was lower for V+N than prep+N when bolded (17.91% vs. 30.91%, z=-4.78, p<.001, Tables 15 & 19; p. 130 prose reverses this direction) but not unbolded (15.80% vs. 17.96%, z=-0.24, p=.99; interaction z=3.08, p=.002, Table 17). Section 5.3.6 (p. 163) explicitly states that Experiment 2 partially corroborates Gitsaki’s gap-fill ordering, distinct from general learnability claims (Howarth, 1998b; Ackerman & Chen, 2013), and notes no prior study compared enhanced and unenhanced L2 lexical and grammatical collocation learning. Shipped row 2422 represents only Sonbul & Schmitt (2013) (adj+N/N+N medical collocations), so Gitsaki (1999) is genuinely absent. Catalog and Google Books records (0236, ISBN 1573093890) verify the 1999 primary empirical book and its 275-learner blank-filling study, while its internal numeric rankings (and equivalence to the restricted 1996 thesis, not substituted here) are not independently read from the book body and rest on Toomer’s explicit attribution.

decisions.reason: Toomer (2019) targets Sonbul and Schmitt’s (2013) Experiment 2 (advanced NNS incidental learning of medical collocations), whose core claims are that repeated exposure (input flooding) produces declarative knowledge over control, typographic enhancement (bolding) yields greater declarative knowledge than unenhanced reading, declarative gains persist at delayed post-test (recognition > recall), and declarative and procedural knowledge are dissociated. In Experiment 1 (Chapter 3, Section 3.10.1.1, pp. 89–90), Toomer replicates all four declarative claims for technical collocations, while his procedural priming finding in the reading-only condition after 9 exposures across two days is an explicit dose extension fulfilling Sonbul and Schmitt’s (p. 153) prediction rather than a replication failure. However, Experiment 2 (Chapter 4) is not solely an extension without original-finding comparison: alongside extending to lexical (V+N) versus grammatical (prep+N) collocations, its Research Questions 1–2 (p. 98) conceptually re-test the same exposure and typographic-enhancement claims, and Section 4.8.2 (pp. 140–141) explicitly benchmarks both against Sonbul and Schmitt (2013). Experiment 2 corroborates input-flooding declarative gains for both collocation types (RQ1, p. 140) and the bolding advantage for prep+N collocations (p < .001), but finds no enhancement advantage for V+N collocations (z = -0.86, p = .79; Table 19, p. 130). Both in Section 4.8.2 (p. 141, answering RQ2 with a “partial ‘yes’”) and in the thesis-wide synthesis (Abstract, p. i; Sections 5.1–5.2.1, pp. 149–150), Toomer explicitly contrasts this unexpected null V+N enhancement result with Experiment 1 and Sonbul and Schmitt (2013), yielding a `mixed` whole-target outcome.

decisions.quote: The results of the immediate cued-recall and form-recognition post-tests corroborate Sonbul and Schmitt’s findings: multiple encounters with the collocations produced substantial declarative collocational knowledge, and more declarative knowledge was produced through exposure to typographically-enhanced collocations (with and without glosses) than to typographically-unenhanced collocations.

decisions.reason: Experiment 1 is explicitly identified as the conceptual replication (and extension) of Sonbul and Schmitt (2013), and the author states an explicit overall verdict that it replicated and corroborated Sonbul and Schmitt's findings on declarative collocational knowledge, whereas Experiment 2 is an extension building on Experiment 1 with non-technical collocations.
